response.translation: Is this, then, anything other than menstrual blood [236] and semen? I for my part know of no third thing. But since the substance of the body in those who are generated is from these principles, the strictly first constitution could be said to be not from a preponderance of the bodies mentioned, but from them alone. And yet why do I say 'the strictly first'? For if we recall what kind of six-day-old seed Hippocrates described, we shall know clearly that the innate body still persists in it. For before any nature of bone or vein or artery or nerve or cartilage or ligament appears in the embryo, only the hot innate body is present in them.

For an unformed, soft flesh, like a clot of blood, succeeds the first form of the embryo, having in it certain things which Hippocrates named, as it were, bloody streaks, deriving from the substance of the semen, its whiteness still being present in it; and later, as much alteration continually takes place, an outline of bone and cartilage and ligament and nerve and artery and vein is completed, at which time the innate hot body still remains [237] in the fetuses, but is greatest always and the more so as the fetuses grow. Their innate hot body, which was blood and semen, becomes less, and a variety of acquired bodies is added. For none of the things mentioned is innate to animals, but all are acquired; and if it were at all possible for an animal ever to become wholly of bone or of nerve, the innate heat would in this way be destroyed. But this is impossible; yet it is possible for the substance of the bones and cartilages and ligaments and nerves and arteries to predominate. Animals, at any rate, that have reached extreme old age, having almost the least of the bloody nature, are composed of bones alone and nerves, membranes and ligaments, arteries and veins and cartilages. For of all the parts of the animal, flesh alone is bloody, and this the aged have in the least amount, and it both poor in blood and hard. Of the other parts mentioned none is bloody.
uncertain_greek: ἀλλὰ πλεῖστον ἀεί τε καὶ μᾶλλόν ἐστιν

response.translation: One must not, therefore, simply measure by the bulk of its substance the quantity of the connate body, which, from the most active [238] of the qualities in it, has been named 'innate heat', but must examine the proportion by comparing it with what is not innate. For just as we say that there is much steam in the bath, or, by Zeus, smoke, or some other such thing, not referring simply to the size of the buildings but to the proper air of the bath, so too in the case of man we shall say that the substance of the innate heat is either very great or small, comparing it with the non-innate bodies. For the infant has all its parts most bloody, so that even in the bones something of the kind is apparent. Conversely, old men have all their parts most bloodless, even to the flesh; for in this too there is very little blood. But since the innate hot body was the blood, it would therefore be concluded from these things that the innate hot body is greatest in those who are growing and least in the aged.

So too the semen, composed of the serous moisture and the pneuma within it, is least in the aged and greatest in the bodies of those who are growing, and of these most of all [239] in the youngest, as we demonstrated in the commentaries On Semen. If, then, you raise the difficulty whether the body of those who are growing is easily consumed and flows away? Yet in the case of other things you are not unaware that hot water or oil or any of the things that are moist in this way is wholly dispersed in the shortest time. For neither earth nor stone nor any other of the things cold and dry by nature is so. For in all things that exist there are two qualities most apt for dispersion, moisture and heat, and conversely two for persistence, dryness and coldness; so that it is no wonder if the bodies of children, because of their moisture and heat, are easily transpired, while those of old men are not easily so, since they have their substance congealed by dryness and cold. So, most excellent Lycus, you bring charges about the very things for which you yourself ought to have been rebuked. You have been shown, then, to be ignorant of one of the first lessons, of which none of those who have been properly introduced is ignorant.

For a large amount of a simple substance is judged by the bulk of the body, but of one that is composed of different things [240] by the proportion of the things mixed, as also with the brain or any other of the parts. Thus, at any rate, those who mix wine with water for drinking say that either the wine is more or the water, or neither, when they have arrived at a due proportion of mixture. But no one is so senseless as, having thrown a kotyle of water into a jar of wine, to say that there is more water in the jar than in the small cup, when, as it happens, there are three kyathoi in the latter, one of water and two of wine. Lycus, however, I suppose, even of the remedy called tetrapharmakon, composed of wax, tallow, pitch and resin, all put together in equal amounts, will not say that it has more pitch if someone puts in double the amount of it relative to the others, but here too will examine whether a whole jar is full of the tetrapharmakon remedy or some small dish, and will then say that the jar has much more pitch than the dish, even if the one was made from equal amounts of the four, while the pitch in the dish is double the others.
uncertain_greek: κἂν ὁ μὲν ἐξ ἴσων ἦν

response.translation: If, then, all such errors [241] belong to people who are unable to distinguish what is called 'much' according to proportion and mixture from what is so called simply according to the common measure, it is not in the same manner in which Lycus brought his charge against Hippocrates. For the substance of the innate heat is greatest in those who are growing, relative to the proportion of the other things, and the quality that goes with it likewise, since the proper qualities are inseparable from the substances, just as the powers also are. So, at any rate, if you put into the tetrapharmakon more pitch than in proportion to the others, you will say that not only its substance but also its quality and its power have shown themselves greater, and for this reason also that whatever is fluid of the pitch has been increased. It is clear, then, that according to the three meanings of 'much' written down by Lycus, both the pitch will be said to be more in the tetrapharmakon and the innate heat in animals.
uncertain_greek: καὶ τὸ ὑγρὸν ὅπερ ἂν τῆς πίττης ηὐξῆσθαι

response.translation: And still more, in cases where the things mixed are not blended as wholes through one another as wholes, it is evident that one thing is said to be more than another in the three ways that Lycus stated, as in the case [242] of this drug, which is among the most customary, composed of iris and birthwort and bitter-vetch meal and frankincense, all equal to one another in weight: one could make one of them double and mix it with the others in their equal amounts, for example the birthwort. It is true, then, to say of their mixture that the birthwort is more in substance, in quality and in activity, and prevails over the others. This same thing one might say of the bath too, when it has in it not only the well-tempered air, but has also taken on some smoke and steam. For of these sometimes the smoke can be more, sometimes the steam, just as also the natural air of the bath. But we do not speak of 'simply' by the 'more' according to excess of substance, with which it is necessary that the quality, too, and the activity that proceeds from it increase together. Let it be supposed, then, that the substance of the smoke is greater than that of the other two: you will then rightly say that the quality of the smoke, too, is greater than the quality of the others, and its activity.
uncertain_greek: τὸ δ’ ἁπλῶς οὐ τῷ πλείονι

response.translation: But it is agreed [243] that one quality does not become more than another quality, but more intense, just as also fainter, not less, although such a use of the words is very frequent throughout the whole book and in all the arts. And why need one mention other things, when we have a clear testimony to the argument in fevers themselves, which everyone daily says have sometimes become greater or less than one another, and sometimes that a man is feverish less or more, this one compared with the same man yesterday or today? Since, then, the 'more' according to quality is assumed to be said in this way, it is no wonder that, in a bath in which there is more substance of smoke, one says that both the quality and the activity have become more: if we name them properly, strong and more intense; if by catachresis, greater and more. For the smoke will clearly bite the eyes in proportion as it increases in substance too; so that, since the proper qualities and the activities always increase together with the substances, one would truly say that in such a bath the smoke is greatest.
uncertain_greek: τὸν δὲ τοῦδε κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν χθὲς ἢ σήμερον

response.translation: Let it be supposed again, as we were saying, [244] that there is some steam and smoke in the bath, while the proper substance of the air is greatest in proportion, being and becoming the analogue of the innate heat in animals; for now too it will be said that the proper heat in the bath is greatest. Is anything, then, lacking from this in the case of the humours in the animal too, from whose vaporizing comes the warmth that meets those who touch from outside? For one heat is kindled from the blood, another from the phlegm, another from the yellow or the black bile. In children, then, the substance of the blood is greatest according to the proportion of the mixture. For of this one must always remind, as though they were held fast by lethargy, those who babble such things as Lycus wrote; and the quality that increases with it is wholesome and friendly, not distressing and biting to those who touch, and so is the activity, according to which the digestions become neither nidorous nor acid, as in the case of phlegm.
uncertain_greek: ἀτμοῦ τε καὶ καπνοῦ κατὰ τὸ βαλανεῖον ὑπάρχειν
οὖσά τε καὶ γιγνομένη τοῦ τοῖς ζώοις ἐμφύτου θερμοῦ

response.translation: In all the ways, then, most noble Lycus, the innate heat is more in those who are growing, so that Hippocrates made no error, [245] but rather you have been refuted as a malicious detractor. For you have shown from what you wrote that you were not at all introduced by teachers to understand anything of the Hippocratic doctrines, and that you openly bring charges against things of which you know nothing at all; and you were caught making a most ignorant counter-argument, attempting by means of it to overturn the constitution of every art; and, being ignorant of what Plato wrote on these matters, you often contradict yourself, doing harm to the young who, like you, are untrained in logical theory and do not know how to distinguish true arguments from false. On top of all this you were seen to be most audacious and at the same time a babbler, having undertaken to write exegeses of what was said by Hippocrates without first having learned it.
